figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: (a) PaperScorer is a family of models trained to predict a paper’s accept/reject decision from either a pure text or a visual view of the paper. (b) For training and evaluation, we built two fully anonymized datasets, sourced from OpenReview and arXiv and labeled with accept/reject decisions. (c) Across training recipes, we find fine-tuning on our large-scale corpora enables PaperScorer to exceed frontier models (GPT/Gemini), specifically on highly rated papers.
figures.headline: PaperScorer models trained on large corpora exceed frontier GPT and Gemini models, especially on highly rated papers.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Dataset mosaic. Screenshots of pages from ICLR and arXiv. ICLR examples use latest-rebuttal OpenReview PDFs, while arXiv examples are derived from LaTeX source, recompiled with venue-specific anonymization macros. Each example tiles multiple pages for visualization; in practice, PaperScorer-Vision processes individual pages. Notably, ICLR papers can contain rebuttal-era revisions (colored text), whereas source-rendered arXiv papers do not.
figures.headline: Anonymized ICLR and arXiv page screenshots show that ICLR pages can retain colored rebuttal-era revisions while arXiv pages do not.
citing_sentences: All datasets are balanced 50/50, and Figure 2 shows examples from both.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Dataset coverage. We summarize the balanced PaperScorer pools by ICLR year and arXiv venue after anonymous recompilation and filtering. ICLR coverage leans toward later years, while arXiv coverage is largest for NeurIPS, CVPR, and ACL-style NLP venues, with smaller balanced slices from other ML conferences.
figures.headline: ICLR coverage leans toward later years, while arXiv coverage is largest for NeurIPS, CVPR, and ACL-style NLP venues.
citing_sentences: The coverage plot in Figure 3 reflects this sampling choice.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Feature-probe audit. (a) The table reports top standardized logistic-regression weights from separate ICLR- and arXiv-trained models, with weights in parentheses. (b) The plots show accepted and rejected paper distributions for the top three accept-associated features within each source on held-out ICLR and arXiv papers. In feature names, per pg. means per estimated body page. Full feature definitions are in Appendix C.
figures.headline: Accept-associated features are mainly paper length, references, and figures, while reject-associated features are more lexical.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 shows that accept features generally have to do with paper length, references, and figures, while reject features are more lexical (full inventory in Appendix C).
The main text reports the top five accept- and reject-associated features from separate ICLR and arXiv feature probes in Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Binary SFT is strongest over time. PaperScorer-Text and PaperScorer-Vision use matched-source training. Across years, supervised PaperScorer leads Acc/AUC, vision is strongest, and RL trails prompting frontier models.
figures.headline: Matched-source supervised PaperScorer leads across years, with vision strongest and RL trailing prompted frontier models.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows that the modality and method ordering is stable across years, with PaperScorer-Vision best in every matched-source year, prompting intermediate, and RL weaker.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Scaling effects. Decision accuracy is largely invariant to model size, with 3B models matching 7B Acc, while data scale drives in-domain accuracy, most visibly on arXiv where the 3.4$\times$ pool boost dominates.
figures.headline: Decision accuracy is largely unchanged between 3B and 7B models, while larger training pools raise arXiv accuracy most.
citing_sentences: Model scale changes decision accuracy only modestly once the SFT objective is fixed (Figure 6a).
A paired 95% bootstrap CI reveals that nearly every change in Acc is statistically insignificant (shaded in Figure 6(a)).
Vision is similarly competitive at smaller scale, so in Figure 6b the largest arXiv Acc gain comes from data scale rather than parameter scale.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Vision is strongest on average. Points show the benefit of using vision over text on both datasets.
figures.headline: Vision outperforms text on average across the ICLR and arXiv comparisons.
citing_sentences: It improves over text in the average ICLR/arXiv view (Figure 7) and in almost every dataset-specific comparison (Table J.2).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Calibration on both datasets. Reliability (confidence vs. accuracy, $y{=}x$ dotted) on the balanced ICLR (left) and arXiv (right) test sets for PaperScorer text and vision and for Jev, after temperature scaling. Dashed lines show the cumulative coverage (share of test papers at or above each confidence).
figures.headline: After temperature scaling, PaperScorer confidence tracks accuracy on both ICLR and arXiv, and Jev is roughly calibrated too.
citing_sentences: After scaling, both PaperScorer models track the $y{=}x$ line on both datasets (Figure 8), so their confidence matches their accuracy, and Jev, corrected the same way, is roughly calibrated too (ECE $.05$ and $.02$, vs. $.02$–$.03$ for ours).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Accuracy of PaperScorer-Vision across reviewer rating. Rating percentile is a paper’s percentile rank in $[0,1]$ among the papers of its own conference and year. (a) Frontier models recognize low-rated papers but fail on the high-rated ones, whereas PaperScorer-Vision is accurate at both tails, while all models are weak in the middle. (b) The same shape as a confidence/rating surface, with a deep dip in the $[0.4,0.5]$ rating slice and the high-accuracy, high-confidence region concentrated on the tail papers.
figures.headline: PaperScorer-Vision is accurate on the lowest and highest rated papers, while all models are near chance in the middle.
citing_sentences: ICLR has human ground-truth ratings for each paper, so we can measure accuracy at each level of the human rating (Figure 9a).

Conditioning jointly on rating and confidence (Figure 9b) shows the same shape, with accuracy peaking on the confident extremes and collapsing in the middle, where none of the evaluated models finds enough signal.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Accuracy by venue. The best frontier vision models (Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.5) against PaperScorer-Vision on arXiv by venue. PaperScorer leads on all high-coverage venues but CVPR and ICCV, where Gemini ties or leads.
figures.headline: PaperScorer-Vision matches or beats the best frontier model on most arXiv venues, with frontier models stronger on CVPR and ICCV.

abstract: Automated research is largely evaluated by benchmark performance, but the value of research rarely reduces to a single score. Humans judge a work's holistic contribution through peer review, which is hard to model because it is noisy and depends on many factors. However, what if, given only the paper, we could predict its peer-review decision directly? We introduce PaperScorer, a family of models that predict a paper's accept or reject decision from its extracted text or page screenshots, training only on the decision after removing author identity and formatting shortcuts. Vision models are the most predictive (68% accuracy on ICLR papers and 77% on ML papers from arXiv), beating text-only and frontier reasoning models. Unlike plain text, page images retain figures, layout, and presentation. This signal is robust, surviving smaller models and even compressing the whole paper into a single image. But accurate predictions are not evenly spread. PaperScorer is strongest on the lowest and highest rated papers, while papers rated in the middle stay unpredictable for our models and frontier systems alike. Additionally, its confidence is calibrated, so its most confident predictions are also its most accurate. Overall, PaperScorer shows how much of the decision a paper carries on its own, marking a first step toward AI-driven research evaluation.

sections.body: The section motivates the question of how predictable a final peer-review decision is from paper content alone. It cites a NeurIPS consistency experiment in which roughly half of papers accepted by one committee would not be accepted by the other, and notes reviewer noise and LLM edits to reviews. The authors introduce PaperScorer, models trained on balanced, anonymized ICLR and arXiv papers as text or page screenshots. Reported results include 68% accuracy on ICLR for PaperScorer-Vision, 2.7% above the best frontier baseline, and 77% on arXiv, 9.0% above frontier baselines. Accuracy stays near chance on papers with intermediate reviewer ratings.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Paper text alone carries recoverable accept/reject signal, but final decisions are noisy and the signal is limited.

sections.body: The authors define the predictor as a text-generation task with an Accept or Reject target, and an acceptance score from normalized decision-token probabilities. Reviews and ratings are not regressed on. The practical target is `p(Z | X_reb)`, the post-rebuttal paper. A Beta-Bernoulli model fitted loosely to one historical NeurIPS consistency experiment gives a Bayes-optimal accuracy of approximately 83.3% under the original acceptance distribution and 80.2% on a balanced evaluation. The authors state that 80.2% is a soft reference point, not a hard limit, because the estimate is loose and rests on one experiment.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: The task is framed as predicting the final decision from the post-rebuttal paper, with a Bayesian ceiling estimate.

sections.body: ICLR contains 25K submissions from OpenReview, evaluated on '25 to '26, and excludes '24 because its accepts are camera-ready. arXiv uses an 83K set and a 25K set, with implied rejects defined as LaTeX-compiling papers absent from venue proceedings. Papers are normalized with MinerU, with author-identifying spans and references removed. Text models receive markdown up to a fixed maximum context length, and vision models receive page screenshots, each rendered and downscaled to a fixed pixel budget. Balanced training reduces the accept-minus-reject recall gap; for example, the ICLR vision gap moves from -9.2 with natural training to +1.8 with balanced training. The models are Qwen2.5 and Qwen2.5-VL backbones, trained with SFT and GRPO-based RL.
sections.heading: PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods
sections.headline: Balanced ICLR and arXiv corpora were built with anonymization and shortcut controls, and training uses balanced labels.

sections.body: Table 3 compares PaperScorer 7B checkpoints with prompted frontier models, coding agents, and DeepReview on ICLR and arXiv. The vision row beats its text row on both datasets, with a paired bootstrap gain at p=.012 for ICLR and .005 for arXiv after Holm-Bonferroni correction. A panel model that tiles ten pages into one image cuts vision tokens by 63% and lowers ICLR accuracy from 68.3 to 66.1. Model scale changes accuracy only modestly, and data scale drives the larger arXiv gain. The authors note that the vision advantage is a conjecture about overall paper appearance, not a settled explanation.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: PaperScorer-Vision outperforms frontier baselines, and vision beats text on both datasets.

sections.body: Temperature scaling makes both PaperScorer models track the diagonal on both datasets, with ECE of .05 and .02 for Jev and .02 to .03 for PaperScorer. At 70% confidence or more, PaperScorer covers about a third of ICLR papers and over half of arXiv papers, at nearly 80% and 85% accuracy. Accuracy is highest on the lowest and highest rated ICLR papers and near chance in the middle of the rating range, where no evaluated model finds enough signal. At ICLR's natural acceptance rate, Accept calls are right 47% of the time and Reject calls 82%. Venue-level accuracy varies, with frontier models tying or leading on CVPR and ICCV.
sections.heading: Where does this signal lie?
sections.headline: Confidence is calibrated, but accuracy is high only at the rating extremes and concentrated in confident predictions.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into paper acceptance prediction, review generation and reviewer agents, and AI-assisted scientific workflows. It names PeerRead, Deep Paper Gestalt, DeepReview, ScholarPeer, and AI Scientist as sources. The authors argue that prior datasets can let labels be recovered from source, venue, or revision artifacts, such as workshop papers used as rejects. They state that PaperScorer is built so the label is recoverable only from paper content. They also frame a calibrated acceptance prior as useful for agentic reviewing and selection pipelines.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work includes paper outcome prediction and reviewer agents, and this work targets label leakage in datasets.

sections.body: The authors state that PaperScorer is not a replacement for peer review or a measure of scientific value. In literature retrieval, combining embedding retrieval scores with the PaperScorer-Vision acceptance score improves ground-truth citation recall in the top-10 results by 8.7% on the LitSearch benchmark. In agentic reviewing, conditioning Claude Code on the PaperScorer-Vision prior raises decision accuracy from 63.0% to 70.6%. The authors describe these applications as uses of a calibrated estimate of acceptance probability as a prior within larger workflows.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Applications
sections.headline: PaperScorer gives a calibrated acceptance prior that improves literature retrieval and agentic reviewing.

sections.body: The authors state that attention maps and section-edit tests do not establish causality, and that the attention analysis rests on a few papers. The model gives no explanation for its predictions, and high acceptance scores do not measure novelty or impact. On ICLR '25, the acceptance score tracks later citations about as well as human review scores, with rho of about .25 for both, though this is one conference-year with a small sample. The model weakens on the newest papers, where data is thin. Dropping '26 from training lowers accuracy, and some '26 decisions may reflect AI help.
sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.headline: Causal claims, explanation, and performance on the newest papers remain unresolved limitations.

sections.body: Appendix A derives the Bayes-optimal ceiling from the NeurIPS consistency experiment and gives the balanced value of 80.2%. Appendix B audits shortcut signals across public datasets, reports artifact availability across OpenReview venues, and explains why ICLR '24 is excluded. Table B.2 shows the selected PaperScorer years have at most 0.92% accepts and 1.73% rejects on any leakage signal. Appendix L describes attention maps and section-level edits scored by PaperScorer-Text, with a 30-paper borderline set and Codex-generated edits. Edit success varies by section, with Formalization and Narrative edits showing the largest effects in different sections.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the Bayesian ceiling derivation, data curation and shortcut audits, and edit-based perturbation analyses.
